concepts.label: new pattern
concepts.title: Event-driven status
concepts.summary: A status change is sent as a small event the moment it happens, instead of waiting for the weekly batch. It replaces the spreadsheet round trip.
concepts.plain: When a lead changes a status, everyone sees it within seconds instead of waiting for the weekly sheet.
concepts.before: A lead pasted the status into a weekly sheet, so everyone saw it days later.
concepts.now: The change is sent the moment it happens and shows on the status page in seconds.
concepts.why: People stop asking where the project stands and trust what they see.
concepts.analogy: A group chat notification instead of a weekly newsletter.

concepts.label: new component
concepts.title: Aggregator
concepts.summary: A worker that reads status events and writes the latest status and the history. It does not serve pages; the API does.
concepts.plain: A behind-the-scenes helper that listens for status changes and keeps the page's data up to date.
concepts.before: A weekly job copied the sheet into an email.
concepts.now: One helper turns each change into stored status and history, and also writes the weekly report.
concepts.why: One place does the bookkeeping, so the page and the report always agree.
concepts.analogy: A librarian who files every new card the moment it arrives.

concepts.label: behavior change
concepts.title: Status history, no overwrite
concepts.summary: Before, an update overwrote the old status. Now every update adds a row, so reports can show what changed and when.
concepts.plain: Instead of erasing the old status, we keep every change so we can see what changed and when.
concepts.before: A new status replaced the old one, and the old one was lost.
concepts.now: Every update adds a line to a history, and the latest line is the one shown.
concepts.why: Reports can show what changed this week, and mistakes can be traced.
concepts.analogy: A bank statement: new lines are added, old ones are never erased.
